title: Poor Feeding
diagnosis: Failure to Thrive (FTT) or Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) are common considerations for Poor Feeding of unknown cause in pediatric patients.
correct_orders: Obtain a thorough history, including feeding habits, weight gain, vomiting, and bowel movements
Physical examination to assess growth parameters, signs of dehydration, abdominal distension, or other relevant findings
Investigations such as complete blood count (CBC), chemistry panel, urinalysis, stool studies, and electrolytes to rule out potential underlying causes like infections, metabolic disorders, or anemia
Consider a swallowing study (videofluoroscopy) or pH monitoring if GERD is suspected
Refer the patient to a pediatric gastroenterologist for further evaluation and management
should_avoid: Initiate aggressive treatment (e.g., antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors) without proper investigations as the underlying cause may not be related to an infection or GERD.

rationale.Initiate aggressive treatment: It is essential to avoid making premature assumptions and starting unnecessary treatments. The diagnosis should first be established through a thorough history, physical examination, and appropriate investigations.
rationale.Oxygen: To provide supplemental oxygen and help maintain adequate oxygenation in the patient with poor feeding
rationale.IV access x2: To establish two large-bore IV access for fluid administration, medication delivery, and blood draws
rationale.glucose check: To quickly assess the blood glucose level of the patient to rule out hypoglycemia as a possible cause of poor feeding

physical_exam: Poor Feeding — exam tailored to chief complaint on arrival.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
